Kafka Streams vs Redis aggregation benchmark

A1 Kafka Streams, streams protocolA2 Kafka Streams, classic protocolB Kafka consumers + Redis

Generated 2026-10-27 13:42 UTC from 68 runs in results/runs. Values are median [min–max] (n repetitions); latency is end-to-end from the broker append time of the latest required fragment to the durable PostgreSQL commit, exact percentiles over all actions. “Worst path” is the highest of the INDIVIDUAL, STAGE2 and FINAL paths. Runs with correctness FAIL are excluded from performance summaries.

Recommendation

No variant met the 500 ms p99.95 SLO in every executed target-load scenario (A1 Streams: FAIL, A2 Classic: FAIL, B Redis: FAIL), so none can be recommended as is for the stated requirement.

Relative to each other, B Redis had the lowest p99.95 in every executed pod-disruption scenario (rolling, abrupt-pod, cold-pod, rescheduling), each time with non-overlapping repetition ranges and at least 10% difference. For the question “which variant processes most reliably under frequent pod rescheduling”, the measured answer on this environment is B Redis; it still exceeds the 500 ms p99.95 SLO, so meeting the SLO requires changes beyond the choice of variant.

Between the two Kafka Streams variants (identical code, different rebalance protocol): A2 Classic was clearly ahead in 4 and A1 Streams in 0 of 4 pod-disruption scenarios (same rule: non-overlapping ranges, ≥ 10%).

Steady-state (S1) end-to-end tails do not separate the variants (overlapping ranges). Variant differences inside the aggregation step are visible in the aggregation-only latency row; docs/ANALYSIS-NOTES.md records where the end-to-end steady-state tails arise.

A late event is an incoming event whose own durable result (INDIVIDUAL action) committed more than 500 ms after the broker appended it. Late events added = late events among actions in flight during the 120 s after the fault, minus what the same run produces without a fault over that time (S5: per replacement; its recovery time is the slowest of the six). Normal-operation noise (shared PostgreSQL stalls) makes small values imprecise and can make them negative; the > 2 s and > 10 s counts are gross and hardly affected by it. Method and decision use: docs/DISRUPTION-IMPACT.md.

Findings (derived from the data above)

  • Best steady-state latency (S1 p99.95 worst path, ms): no clear winner — A2 Classic 1,181.1 vs A1 Streams 1,364.5 (difference 13%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Lowest aggregation-only latency (S1 p99.95, append → executor pickup, ms): B Redis (110.1) ahead of A2 Classic (541.9), difference 80%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Highest sustained throughput (S1, fragments/s): no clear winner — A1 Streams 5,957.0 vs B Redis 5,956.0 (difference 0%; repetition ranges overlap).
  • Lowest rolling-upgrade latency (S2 p99.95, ms): B Redis (2,954.9) ahead of A2 Classic (10,169.8), difference 71%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest failure-induced latency, abrupt pod kill (S3 p99.95, ms): B Redis (10,586.0) ahead of A2 Classic (15,755.6), difference 33%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest failure-induced latency, cold replacement (S4 p99.95, ms): B Redis (1,932.6) ahead of A2 Classic (3,852.8), difference 50%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Lowest latency under frequent rescheduling (S5 p99.95, ms): B Redis (2,088.1) ahead of A2 Classic (5,981.4), difference 65%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per rollout (S2): B Redis (36,927.0) ahead of A2 Classic (167,093.0), difference 78%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per abrupt pod failure (S3): B Redis (40,727.0) ahead of A2 Classic (96,899.0), difference 58%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Fewest late events added per cold pod replacement (S4): B Redis (7,704.0) ahead of A1 Streams (50,215.0), difference 85%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Shortest partition stall after abrupt failure (S3, ms): B Redis (11,489.0) ahead of A2 Classic (15,895.0), difference 28%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.
  • Shortest partition stall during rolling upgrade (S2, ms): B Redis (2,774.0) ahead of A2 Classic (7,420.0), difference 63%, non-overlapping repetition ranges.

Recovery reliability

  • A1 Streams: 22 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.
  • A2 Classic: 22 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.
  • B Redis: 24 runs, correctness failures: 0; runs whose latency did not return under the SLO within the fault window: 0.

State size

  • A1 Streams: state-1s: restore 2,100 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 7,738 (n=1) ms; state-10s: restore 2,387 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 10,329 (n=1) ms; state-60s: restore 4,504 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 9,696 (n=1) ms. First tested window where the failure-window p99.95 exceeds 500 ms: state-1s.
  • A2 Classic: state-1s: restore 156 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 2,107 (n=1) ms; state-10s: restore 267 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 4,960 (n=1) ms; state-60s: restore 232 (n=1) ms, failure p99.95 3,641 (n=1) ms. First tested window where the failure-window p99.95 exceeds 500 ms: state-1s.
  • B Redis (for comparison): state-1s: failure p99.95 2,316 (n=1) ms; state-10s: failure p99.95 1,393 (n=1) ms; state-60s: failure p99.95 2,747 (n=1) ms.

Resource cost (S1)

  • A1 Streams: aggregators 2.08 cores / 2,584 MiB; Kafka broker 0.46 cores / 2,048 MiB.
  • A2 Classic: aggregators 1.74 cores / 2,605 MiB; Kafka broker 0.45 cores / 2,048 MiB.
  • B Redis: aggregators 2.13 cores / 907 MiB; Kafka broker 0.32 cores / 1,578 MiB, Redis 0.36 cores / 1,360 MiB.

Kafka Streams pays for state durability with changelog writes and one standby replica per task (extra broker load and RocksDB memory in the aggregator pods); B pays with a separate Redis server.

Recovery after injected failures

State size and restoration (S6)

Resource consumption (steady)

Limitations of this environment

  • Single OrbStack node: all pods share one VM, one disk and one kernel; node failures, cross-node networking, rack awareness and independent failure domains are not reproduced.
  • The local profile has one Kafka broker and one Redis node; broker failover and Redis replication are only exercised in the HA profile (./scripts/deploy.sh --ha).
  • Other workloads on the same cluster share CPU and memory; runs whose node CPU p95 exceeded 90% are marked INCONCLUSIVE.
  • All timestamps come from the same node clock; cross-machine clock skew is not present here but would be in production.
  • All variants write their actions to one shared PostgreSQL instance on the same VM, so stalls of that write path appear in every variant's end-to-end latency (aggregation-only latency excludes it).
  • Steady and failure windows are assigned by the broker append time of an action's source fragment; an action appended shortly before a fault and delayed by it counts as steady. Whole-window figures (used for S2–S5 above) do not depend on this rule; its effect per run is quantified by scripts/analysis/window_sensitivity.py (see docs/ANALYSIS-NOTES.md).

Raw data

Per run: verification.json (all statistics and correctness checks), per_second_latency.csv, lag.csv, throughput.csv, producer.csv, timeline.csv, latencies.csv.gz (every action), resources.json, logs and startup configuration reports. Summary: results/summary.csv.
